claims.text: Introducing a gradient heterostructure with ultra-fine surface grains and relatively coarse interior grains can overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in metals.
A homogeneous fine-grained microstructure exhibits high strength but low ductility.
Surface mechanical attrition treatment followed by controlled annealing can generate an ultra-fine-grained surface layer over a coarse-grained core.
A grain-size gradient creates regions with distinct deformation behaviors.
Interfaces between ultra-fine and coarse-grained regions facilitate strain partitioning.
The ultra-fine-grained regions provide high strength.
Strain incompatibility at interfaces promotes the accumulation of geometrically necessary dislocations.
The accumulation of geometrically necessary dislocations enhances strain hardening and accommodates plastic deformation.
The gradient heterostructure will have higher yield strength than a homogeneous fine-grained baseline.
The gradient heterostructure will have significantly greater ductility than a homogeneous fine-grained baseline.
The benefits of the gradient heterostructure may be limited under very high strain-rate conditions.
An excessively steep microstructural gradient may lead to interfacial failure.
The optimal gradient profile and processing conditions are not fully determined and require experimental optimization.
